terms.gloss: a leader, a guide; in war, a commander
terms.grammar: noun, third declension, masculine or feminine
evidence: Cic. de Or. 3.63: dux regendae cīvitātis (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The general word for whoever leads a group, a party or an army, and feminine as well: dux fēmina factī (Verg. A. 1.364, Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: the leading man; in the plural, the leaders of a people
evidence: Caes. BG 1.30.1: tōtīus ferē Galliae lēgātī, prīncipēs cīvitātum
terms.comment: Under the emperors, the emperor’s own title, chosen by Augustus.

terms.gloss: one who steers: the leader of a state
evidence: Cic. Rep. 2.52: rēctor et gubernātor cīvitātis (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: From the helmsman (Lewis & Short); Morgan–Owens has it for the leader of a nation.
Classical prose has it (Cicero, Livy), but it is above all a favourite word of Vergil’s, who uses it more than twenty times (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: Cloelia virgō ūna ex obsidibus … frūstrāta custōdēs, dux agminis virginum inter tēla hostium Tiberim trānāvit
phrases.english: Cloelia, a girl who was one of the hostages, slipped past her guards and, at the head of a band of girls, swam the Tiber under the enemy’s spears

sources: Lewis & Short: dux · Lewis & Short: princeps · Lewis & Short: rector · Lewis & Short: ductor
